WRITTEN ANSWERSTO STARRED QUESTIONS 
National Highways in Assam 
*221. SHRIDWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Will the Minister of ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have sanctioned any amount for construction and 
widening of various National Highways in Assam; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the details of the funds likely to be released for the purpose? 
 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS [MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI]: 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) During 2002-2003, 44 improvement works including widening 
amounting to Rs. 146 crore have been sanctioned for the development of various 
National Highways in the State of Assam. 
(c) During 2002-2003, an amount of Rs. 149.37 crore has been allocated 
for the development of National Highways in the State of Assam. 
Separate account for different services 
*222. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Telecom Regulatory Authority of India has ordered phone 
companies to maintain separate account for different services they provide; 
4 

[6 March, 2003]                  RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether TRAI has taken any steps to ensure prevention of cross-
subsidisation by phone companies; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRIARUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Government has notified "Telecom Regulatory Authority of 
India, Service Providers (Maintenance of Books of Accounts and other 
Documents) Rules, 2002" under which telecom service providers are required 
to maintain books of accounts to reflect service-wise operational expenses, 
revenues and fixed assets. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) In accordance with the provisions of Telecommunication Tariff Order 
(TTO), 1999, all operators are required to report tariffs to the Telecom Regulatory 
Authority of India (TRAI). This requirement provides an opportunity to 
TRAI to monitor the tariffs with respect to cross subsidisation, predatory 
pricing, etc. TRAI intervenes on tariffs either suo moto or on the basis of a 
reference to it from any affected party on specified grounds including cross 
subsidisation. Further, TRAI has also formulated a System on Accounting 
Separation (SAS) which would assist in identifying cross subsidisation 
practices. 
Status of SSIs 
*223. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the present status of the small scale industries, so far as production and 
employment generation are concerned; 
(b) whether the reforms process has weakend the small scale industry sector; 
and 
(c) if not, how the structural reforms have strengthened these industries so far 
as their economic viability is concerned? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) The present status of Small Scale Industries (SSI) in terms

of estimated production and employment for the year 2001 -02 (latest 
available) is as under:- 
Year Production (Rs. crore) Employment (lakh Nos.)  
2001-02 6,90,316 192.23 
(b) and (c) The structural reforms initiated by the government which 
include liberalisation and globalisation, have had mixed impact on the Small 
Scale Industries (SSI) in India. While these have exposed the SSI sector to 
greater competition both domestically and globally on one hand, they have on the 
other provided the SSI sector greater access to markets, cheaper imported raw 
materials and technologies. The SSI sector has demonstrated the resilience to 
withstand the competition as it has recorded a rate of growth, which is higher 
than the overall industrial growth. 
Assistance to Singapore in combating terrorism 
*224. SHRIRAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Singapore has sought India's assistance in effectively 
combating terrorism; and 
(b) if so, the mutual facilitation of the security services proposed to 
contain the threat of terrorism? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) No, Sir. However, in view of 
the common concerns regarding terrorism, India and Singapore have had 
periodic exchange of views on this matter, including ongoing cooperation 
between the security agencies of the two countries. 
Issuance of Passports 
*225. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of passports issued by Regional Passport Offices in the 
country during the last five years and till date, Regional Passport Office-wise 
and State-wise; 
(b) the average time taken by passport offices in issuing passports; 
6 

[6 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) the number of applications pending for issuance of passports in the 
different passport offices during the last one year; and 
(d) the measures taken or proposed to be taken by Government to dispose 
these applications expeditiously? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) A statement (Statement-I) is 
placed (See below). 
(b) The average time taken for issuing a passport is six weeks provided 
clear police verification report has been received and documentation of 
applicant is complete. 
(c) A statement (Statement-II) is placed (See below).The number of 
pendencies has come down significantly to 83,877 in 2002 from 3,43,487 in 
2000. 
(d) Measures taken for the expeditious disposal of pending 
applications include expediting police verification reports, ensuring that 
passport applications are received complete, computerisation of Passport 
Offices, machine writing of passports, decentralisation of receipt of 
passport applications and weekly monitoring of the pendency.

Statement 
Steps taken by the Government to promote the Information Technology 
Sector 
1. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) has been 
rationalized and extended uniformly to all sectors without any 
threshold limit on payment of 5% duty. 
2. Approvals for all foreign direct investment prof. :sals relating to the 
Information Technology sector, with the exception c? Business-to-
consumer (B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic route. 
3. Electronics Hardware Technology  Park (EHTP) and Software 
Technology Park (STP) Schemes are implemented under the aegis of the 
Department of Information Technology, Ministry of Communications 
and Information Technology, through a single window mechanism of 
the Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee (IMSC). 
4. Supplies of Information Technology Agreement (ITA-I) items in the 
Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) by EHTP/EOU/EPZ units shall be 
counted towards fulfillment of minimum Net Foreign 
Exchange earning as a Percentage of exports (NFEP)  and the 
minimum Export Performance (EP), provided that the items are 
manufactured in the unit and attract zero rate of basic customs duty. 
Postive NFEP is required to be achieved in 5 years instead of every 
year. 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2003] 
5. DTA access upto 50% of th FOB value of export is permitted for electronics 
hardware units under EOU/EPZ/EHTP schemes arid the software units 
under EOU/EPZ/STP schemes. 
6. Accelerted depreciation norms extended to computers and computer 
peripherals to all units and capital goods of IT hardware units under Export 
Oriented schemes (EOU/EPZ/STP/EHTP). These shall stand depreciated to 
overall limit of 90% over a period of 3 years. 
7. Special Economic Zones are being set up to enable hassle free 
manufacturing and trading for export purposes. 
8. The Depreciation on Computers is allowed @ 60%. 
9. In the Budget 2002-03, the peak rate of customs duty has been reduced 
from 35% to 30%. Customs duty has been reduced on stepper motors for 
computers/printers from 5% to 0%, floppy diskette and unrecorded 
magnetic tape from 15% to 10%, ink cartridges/ribbon assembly/ribbon 
gear assembly/ribbon gear carriage for use in printers for computers from 
25% to 5%, 56 items of capital goods for manufacture of semiconductors 
from 5% to 0%, 24 items of capital goods for manufacture of electronic 
components from 25-35% to 15%, tools/moulds/dies for electronics 
industry from 25% and on 46 items of raw materials for manufacture 
of electronic components from 25-35% to 5%. 
Customs duty on Computers and Peripherals continues to be @ 15% and 
all storage devices, Integrated circuits, microprocessors, data display tubes 
and deflection components of colour monitor continue at 0%. The 
concessional rate of customs duty @ 5% for specified raw materials for 
the electronics industry (121 items) continues. Customs duty on 
Information Technology Agreement (ITA -I) items of WTO (IT and 
Telecom products) contiues @ 15%, parts of Telecom continue @ 5%,

cellular telephohes continue at 0%

under DPE guidelines or the Voluntary Retirement Scheme which was prevailing 
in the company prior to disinvestment whichever is more beneficial for the 
employees. It is interesting to note that while much is made of the likely adverse 
impact of disinvestment on employment, public sector undertakings have seen a 
net reduction in employment from a level of 2.179 million employees in 1991 -92 
to a level of 1.806 million in 1999-2000, as reported by DPE Survey 2000-01. In 
contrast, the loss of direct employment in disinvested PSUs has been marginal 
while in one case net employment has increased. In several cases, the new 
management has finalized pending wage agreements and wages and allowances 
have increased substantially. Disinvestment is expected to facilitate the productive use 
of assets and thus contribute to growth and employment. There is anecdotal 
evidence that efficiency enhancement has been achieved by disinvested PSUs, 
which is beneficial for the economy and for employment. 
(c) Profitability is not synonymous with efficiency. Often PSUs are 
profitable more on account of administered pricing or monopoly status, rather 
than the efficiency of the operations. There have been many cases where 
profitable PSUs have become loss making after liberalisation and increased 
competition. The sale of loss making PSUs alone will not generate the 
resources required by the Government for modernization 
26 

[6 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
and upgradation of PSUs, creation of new assets, generations of employment 
and retiring of public debt. Further, the disinvestment of profitable non-
strategic PSUs would insulate government finances from the commercial and 
business risk associated with owning a company and separate the regulatory 
functions of government from the production and supply of services and 
products.

1. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) has been

Information Technology sector, with  the exception of Business-to-
consumer (B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic route.

aegis of the Department o f Information Technology, Ministry of 
Communications and Information Technology, through a single window 
mechanism of the Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee (IMSC).

software units under EOU/EPZ/STP schemes. 
5. Accelerated depreciation norms applicable to computers and computer 
peripherals for units under Export Oriented 
schemes(EOU/EPZ/EHTP/STP). These shall stand depreciated to 
overall limit of 90% over a period of 3 years.

magnetic tape from 15% to 10% and on ink cartridges/ ribbon

for computers from 25% to5%. Customs duty on Computers and 
Peripherals continues to be @ 15% and all storage devices, integrated 
circuits, microprocessors, data display tubes and deflection 
components of colour monitors continue at 0%. Customs duty on 
Information Technology Agreement (ITA-1) items of WTO (IT and

Excise Duty. 
9. Second hand capital goods upto 10 years are freely importable.

Import of edible oil 
1603. SHRINANDIYELLAIAH: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether edible oil imports are likely to rise in the crop year to 
October, with winter oilseed production having fallen from a year earlier; 
(b) if so, whether due to poor production, Government are considering to 
import more edible oils this year; 
(c) if so, what is the target set for import of edible oils; and 
(d) what are the steps being taken to improve edible oil production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRIV. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) There is a persistent gap between demand and domestic supply 
of edible oils. The domestic supply depends on oilseed production which has 
declined substantially according to estimates of Ministry of Agriculture. 
Hence the net domestic availability of edible oils is expected to be less than the 
last year. The Government, with a view to ensure availability of edible oils in 
the domestic market, has allowed import of edible oils except coconut oil 
under Open General Licence (OGL). As such, the import of edible oils would 
depend upon the commercial judgement of the importers. There is no 
proposal, at present, to import edible oils on Government account. 
(d) Some of the steps taken and efforts made to increase the indigenous 
production of oilseeds and hence of edible oils include: 
(i) A Centrally Sponsored Oilseeds Production Programme is 
implemented in 25 State covering 395 selected Districts to increase the 
production of oilseeds/edible oils in the country. 
(ii) A Technology Mission on Oilseeds is in place to harness best 
production, processing and management technology. 
(iii) Intensification of research efforts to increase the production of 
oilseeds. 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2003] 
(iv) Increasing the areas under non-traditional oilseeds crops, like Soyabean and 
Sunflower and exploitation of oilseeds of tree and forest origin, rice bran etc. 
(v) Setting up of necessary processing and infrastructural facilities to keep pace 
with the production programme of oilseeds. 
(vi) Assistance for oil palm development. 
(vii) Better incentives to producers through fixation of Minimum Support 
Price (MSP) of major oilseeds. 
(viii) Use of indigenous oils in the manufacture of Vanaspati to at least 25% of 
the production, on a monthly basis, is mandatory, at present. Higher use of expeller 
Mustard oil in the manufacture of Vanaspati up to 30% has also been allowed. The 
objective is to incentives the farmers in terms of better returns for their production. 
(ix) In order to harmonise the interest of domestic oilseeds growers, consumers 
and processors and to regulate imports of edible oils to the extent possible, the duty 
structure on edible oils is reviewed from time to time.

With respect to the question whether the provisions of the Article 13.4 of 
the Agreement to Sell between BHPL and Hotel Corporation of India (HCI) 
have been violated because of the transfer of the entire shareholding by the 
then shareholders of BHPL to SIG without the consent of HCI, the Learned 
AG has opined that it is a well-established principle that a company is a body 
corporate distinct from its members. In other words a company is a juristic 
person and is distinct from its shareholders. Transfer of the entire shareholding by 
the then shareholders of BHPL to the SIG does not in Law amount to an 
"assignment". BHPL is a llegal entity separate from the shareholders. Even 
after the transfer of shareholding, BHPL is obliged to perform the terms and 
conditions of the Agreement to Sell. There has been no assignment by BHPL 
of the "benefits or burdens" of the Agreement to Sell to SIG. Consequently, 
there was no obilgation on BHPL to obtain any prior consent as contemplated 
by Article 13.4 of the Agreement to Sell and there has been no breach by 
BHPL. 
As regards the issue of whether the provisions of the Article 24 of the 
Lease Agreement between BHPL and Airports Authority of India (AAI) have 
been violated because of the transfer of the entire shareholding by the then 
shareholders of BHPL to SIG without the consent of AAI, the Learned AG 
has opined that Article 24 of the Lease Agreement requires prior written 
approval of the Lessor if the Lessee, i.e. BHPL desires to mortgage assign, 
transfer or sublet the leased premises. Transfer of 
110 

[6 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
shareholding of a company does not amount to either a mortgage, 
assignment, transfer or sub-leasing of the land which has been leased. 
Consequently, here was no obligation to obtain prior approval in writing from 
the Lessor, i.e. AAI. Hence, there has been no breach of the Lease Agreement. 
In response to the question of whether BHPL has violated the provisions 
of the Agreemetn to Sell and the Lease Agreement because of change of name 
of the company to SHPL, the Learned AG has advised that it needs to be borne in 
mind that change of name does not affect the entity of the company or its 
countinuity as the same entity. The company remains the same corporate body 
and the change does not affect any of its rights or obligations or render 
defective any legal proceedings by or against it. In the AG's view, this legal 
position is reinforced by Section 23(3) of the Companies Act, 1956 which 
reads as under— 
“The change of name shall not affect any rights or obligations of the 
company, or render defective any legal proceedings by or against it; and 
any legal proceedings which might have been continued or commenced 
by or against the company by its former name may be continued by or 
against the company by its new name.” 
As regards the question of whether any action can be taken against BHPL 
and SHPL to pierce the corporate veil and taking remedial actions for cancelling 
the Agreements, the Learned AG has advised that there is no matrerial which 
establishes fradulent conduct or any illegality in the transactions and 
therefore, the doctrine of piercing the corporate veil would be inapplicable. 
Hence in the AG's opinion, cancellation of the agreements would not be 
warranted.

Sale of 'Navaratanas' 
1617. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether corporate India is opposed to the strategic sale of profit making 
public sector 'Navaratanas' as has been suggested by the FICCI President that 
they be converted autonomous corporation run by the professional 
management; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the value of assets of these undertakings cannot 
be scientifically evaluated or estimated; and 
(c) if so, Government's reaction in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to 
(c) No, Sir. However, the President of the Federation of Indian Chambers of 
Commerce and Industry has made the following suggestions. 
* Government should emulate the UK model of privatisation 
programme, wherein most of the bigger British PSUs were offered to the 
public rather than to the individual strategic owners. 
* Disinvestment should be done through IPO route and Government could 
think of placing shares in the Newyork Stock Exchange and a good 
portion in the domestic market with some reservation for employees. 
118 

[6 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
* PSUs can well become board managed companies which should be able 
to function independently as professionally managed commercial 
entities. 
Emulating the example of any other country, as has been suggested by the 
President of FICCI, is not desirable as the objective conditions may be very 
different. Experience shows that the sales realisation is maximised in the case 
of strategic sale as the private investor pays a premium for the transfer of 
management control. If the Government sells its majority shares through a 
public offer there will always be the possibility that a private investor may 
acquire the company cheaply, through "creeping acquisition", or the purchase 
of shares in small lots from the public, without paying a control premium. It 
also needs to be kept in mind that the majority of PSUs are not listed, even in the 
domestic stock exchanges, and considerable effort and time would need to be 
spent to bring them to a state of preparedness for listing prior to public offer. 
A disinvestment strategic relying on public offer of shares must also be 
viewed in the context of the size, depth and level of integration of the domestic 
capital market with the international capital markets. Keeping these factors in 
view, the Government has adopted a flexible disinvestment strategy, which 
adopts both strategic sale and public offer of shares in the domestic and 
international market, as is appropriate, on a case by case basis. 
The argument that PSUs shoulcrnot be disinvested merely because they are 
profitable cannot be justified. Profitability is not synonymous with efficiency. 
Often PSUs are profitable more on account of administered pricing or monopoly 
status, rather than the efficiency of the operations. There have been many cases 
where profitable PSUs have become loss making after liberalisation ana* 
increased competition. The sale of loss making PSUs alone will not generate 
the resources required by the Government for modernisation and upgradation of 
PSUs, creation of new assets, generation of employment and retiring of public 
debt. Further, the disinvestment of profitable non-strategic PSUs insulates 
Government finances from the commercial and business risk associated with 
owning a company and separate the regulatory functions of Government from 
the production and supply of services and products. 
Valuation of Assets is one of four methodologies used in the 
disinvestment of PSUs and is useful in the case of liquidation of the 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2003] 
companies. Discounted Cash Flow Method, Balance Sheet Method, 
Transaction Multiple Method are more appropriate for valuation of a going 
concern. These valuation methodologies are internationally recognised. On the 
basis of the results obtained using these four separate valuation methodologies, 
the reserve price is determined. The actual sale price, however, is determined 
through a process of competitive bidding, which allows the market determined 
valuation, at that point of time, to be revealed.

SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

cooperation in economic and other fields;

his visit to the New York;

decisions taken during the talks by the two Prime Ministers; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) to (c) Yes. 
(d) During Prime Minister's visit to Japan in December, 2001, it had been 
agreed to hold a regular exchange of views at high levels to facilitate the cross 
sectoral dialogue on bilateral, regional and international issues. Deepened 
economic relations are seen as an essential underpinning to strengthen the 
bilateral relationship. Information and communication technology are areas 
where there are extraordinary strong complementarities between the two 
countries.The comprehensive security dialogue as well as Military-to-Military 
consultations are to be held annually and a dialogue on counter terrorism included

was also agreed to

Prime Ministers during their meeting in New York in September 2002 on the 
sidelines of the UN General Assembly ag reed to further st rengthen relations

2001.

alia, include the following:

2003 to study and review economic co-operation between the two

(a) whether a meeting of National Development Council was held in 
December last; 
(b) if so, issues discussed and the targets fixed for growth; 
(c) the proposed action plan to generate additional employment 
opportunities both in labour intensive and others; and 
(d) the action plan to help States facing alarming fiscal deficit? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) The 50th meeting of the 
National Development Council (NDC) was held on 21st December, 2002. The 
agenda of this meeting was to consider the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002—07).. 
The NDC unanimously approved the Tenth Five Year Plan, which envisages an 
annual average growth rate of 8% of GDP for the Tenth Plan period. 
(c) and (d) The Tenth Plan proposes to generate 50 million employment 
opportunities during the Tenth Plan period. To achieve this objective, it is 
expected that the 8% annual average growth will lead to 30 million 
opportunities through the growth process alone, and another 20 million will be 
created through interventions in specific sectors and activities. The thrust areas 
identified in the Plan include agriculture, irrigation, agro-forestry, small and medium 
enterprises, information communication technology and tourism. The Tenth Plan 
identified fiscal correction as one of the critical areas for improving the 
financial position of the states. Pursuant to the recommendations of the Eleventh 
Finance Commission (EFC), the Ministry of Finance has already drawn up a scheme 
of Medium Term Fiscal Reform Plan (MTFRP), which inter-alia aims at restoring 
the financial health of the State Governments. In addition, a debt swap mechanism 
has been proposed for reducing the interest burden of the States.

Problem of SSIs 
†1692. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI LAJPAT RAI: 
Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the facts 
highlighted by the National Sample Survey Organisation in its 56th report 
regarding the unorganised units in the small scale sector; 
(b) if so, whether the problems being faced by the units in the above 
sector have been highlighted comprehensively in the report alongwith its 
impact; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and their impact on those units? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c)The National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) in its 
56th Round conducted an all India sample survey of unorganized 
manufacturing enterprises comprising those that were not covered under the 
Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) conducted by them. The ASI is conducted 
every year by NSSO to survey all the manufacturing enterprises that are 
registered under Section 2 (m) (i) and 2 (m) (ii) of Factories Act, 1948 and 
under the Bidi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966. 
The main criteria for coverage under ASI is that the manufacturing enterpises 
should be engaging 10 or more workers and using power or engaging 20 or 
more workers and not using power. Since the definition of small scale 
industries (SSI) sector is in terms of upper ceiling of original value of plant 
and machinery, some part of the SSI sector is covered in ASI and another part 
is inter alia covered in the sample survey of unorganized manufacturing. 
Hence, the 56th Round survey conducted by NSSO is not a comprehensive 
survey of the SSI sector. However, the problems being faced by the 
unorganised manufacturing enterprises as reported by the NSSO in its 56th 
Round are shortage of capital, problem of marketing of products, power 
problems, competition from large units etc.
